description: Dependency updates for both halves of this repository, proposed by a bot and merged by a human.

THE SEVEN DAY COOLDOWN IS THE POINT. minimumReleaseAge holds every update back until its version has been public for seven days. The attack this defends against is a package that is compromised, published, and used to harvest credentials from everyone who installs it within hours. Most compromised releases are spotted and pulled within days, so a version that is a week old has survived the window in which almost all of that damage is done. A dependency graph is attack surface and every entry in it runs with our privileges.

The cooldown is not the detection path for a vulnerability that is already known. CI runs cargo audit and pip-audit on every push and fails the build rather than warning, so a dependency with a published advisory is loud immediately whether or not a Renovate branch exists for it yet.
NOTHING AUTOMERGES. The baseline rule is that the bot proposes and a human reviews and approves, so automerge is off everywhere and there is no rule below that turns it back on for a subset.

requirements.lock is ignored on purpose. It is not a lockfile to be kept current: it records the exact environment that produced the published corpus, including the JIT compiler behind the code that decides which pixels carry a payload. Updating it would destroy the record it exists to be.

requirements.txt is pinned to the versions the published numbers were measured against, so an update there is a decision about the measurement rather than routine maintenance. The bot may raise it; a person decides it.

packageRules.description: Rust crates, one pull request rather than a stream of them. The workspace dependency set is deliberately small, so grouping keeps the whole set reviewable in a single read.
Python packages for the generators. Grouped for the same reason, and never merged without someone deciding whether the numbers move.

GitHub Actions, pinned by commit hash rather than by tag. A tag can be repointed at any commit by whoever owns the repository it lives in, which is how the tj-actions/changed-files compromise reached everyone who wrote @v4.
The documentation site's packages. They build a static site and never touch a measurement, so they are grouped and kept out of the way of the two sets that do.
A major version of anything is its own pull request. Grouping a breaking change in with routine bumps is how a breaking change gets waved through.
